utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, please call the case, and let's move.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, assisted by Denise Gustin case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Milan Trbojevic, attorney at law; lead counsel, Mr. John Ackerman; and our colleague Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Good morning to you too. Thank you. Any preliminaries? Yes. I recognise Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I told -- I told Ms. Chuqing there weren't going to be any preliminaries, but I'm just going to tell you this: I'm going to need the same half hour that we had on Monday morning so that we would start at 9.30 to consult with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I can explain why we need to if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But if it's necessary to bring your client a half an hour earlier, it will, you know, make everybody's life easier and it will not take from our sitting time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If they're willing to do that, I'm willing to do that too, Your Honour. The -- part of the problem is like -- for instance, yesterday we wanted to consult with him for about 15 minutes and security would not make that possible. They had to move him rather quickly yesterday. And I understand that. I'm not quarreling with security about that. That's what they have to do; they have to do. But it made it necessary for us to consult with him this morning instead of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we will do, Madam Registrar, please, between now and the end of the sitting, see if on Monday they could bring Mr. Brdjanin half an hour earlier than usual so that Mr. Ackerman can sit down with him at 8.30 -- if it's not possible at 8.30, we'll try quarter to 9.00. But we'll try to keep intact as much as we can the amount of hours we need for the sitting. That's number one. Number two, I went through your response to the Prosecution's motion for judicial notice. I went through it carefully. I -- on a prima facie basis, without, of course, pronouncing myself on the matter. But it seems to me that you may be right -- Have you had a look at it, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour may have noticed I was asking Ms. Gustin. I haven't looked at it. I didn't appreciate that I'd been given a copy of the filing, so I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I will be very succinct. Basically Mr. Ackerman is saying more than one thing, but one of the main things is that it seems to him that most, if not all, of your motion is based on the evidence of six persons. This evidence or the transcript of this evidence is, it seems, not in any way available. He says that he's not actually in a position to respond finally yes or no until or unless he's been put in a position to take notice of -- take cognisance of the contents of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then there is another matter. And I think also prima facie that he is right, that when you ask for judicial notice to be taken of certain facts having taken place in a certain -- taken place in a certain place, as part of the conspiracy of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Criminal enterprise, you're asking two things. You're mixing facts with a legal connotation. Whether they are a matter -- whether they form part of the criminal enterprise is as the legal matter -- he draws the parallel line with other instances where the question of whether there was an international conflict in Bosnia was a fact or whether it was also a point of law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It's a legal conclusion from a set of facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. So I would suggest to you that you look at his response in the light of what I have just said and we'll revisit the matter first thing on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I can very quickly tell you on the problem with -- we wouldn't have the slightest objection giving him the transcripts, although I think Rule 94 was meant to do away with all this necessity if there'd have been a finding. Is that all of them are -- were protected, I think, in the Tadic trial, and therefore we'd need to apply to President Jorda for permission to release under 75, Rule 75, before we can give them to another Defence counsel. And with the greatest respect to the President, who I have no doubt is a very busy man, it seems to take forever to get these motions answered, because we had to do a number of them which arose from Tadic. But that's what I foresee is the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Today is not the right day to file such a -- but if you file it Monday, I think I will do my best to have it responded to as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, then I'll make arrangements for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Because I think once Mr. Ackerman has got access to those -- to the transcript of those six witnesses, he also leaves all doors open in the sense that it may well be that having gone through these transcripts, he -- he may enter in non-opposition later on. So the options are -- the option is there and let's take advantage of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You Honour -- I'll tell Your Honour quite off -- straight off that the reason we -- otherwise we could have applied to put the transcripts in under Rule 92, but our attitude has been that it would be wrong to try to put transcripts in of witnesses we know cannot or will not testify for cross-examination. So that's the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, shall -- anything else before we proceed, move into a closed session? Madam Registrar -- Madam Usher, closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before we pack up for the weekend, I just wanted to express my gratitude and that of the other two Judges on this Trial Chamber to all of you, interpreters and technicians and staff of all sorts for having overstayed by more than 20 minutes. I appreciate that. As a result of that, you have saved the Tribunal some of its resources. I thank you. Monday here, I think, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 2.07 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of November, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
